extracted.intended_audience: patent applicants and patent attorneys filing national Finnish (PRH) patent applications
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for drafting and filing a national patent application before the Finnish Patent and Registration Office (PRH), covering patentable subject matter, required documents, claim drafting, specification content, formalities, publication, appeals and enforcement. Focuses on content, form, timing and procedural requirements for national (and national-phase international/EP) applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility model renewal and maximum protection term
rubrics_metrics.description: Utility model registration must be renewed by paying a renewal fee. The registration may be renewed twice: first for four years and then for two years. The protection period is at most 10 years from the filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Renewal payments and timing are mandatory to keep utility model protection in force (see J.3.6).

rubrics_metrics.name: Publicity and confidentiality of patent and utility model documents
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent documents are public from the patent grant date. Patent application documents become public 18 months from the patent application filing date or earliest priority date. Utility model documents are public from the registration date or at latest 15 months from filing or earliest priority date. Before becoming public, application documents are confidential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PRH publishes made-public patent and utility-model applications and granted patents/utility models. Applicants should be aware of the 18‑month (patents) / 15‑month (utility models) publication timing and confidentiality until then (PatL 22 §; HmL 18 §; PatL 7a § 2 mom.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Availability of published patents/applications in patent databases
rubrics_metrics.description: Published patent and utility model applications, as well as granted patents and utility models, can be searched in patent databases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PRH's patent information service contains data on Finnish patents, utility models and SPCs and related documents; use these databases to inspect public filings and publications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal rights, deadlines and fees
rubrics_metrics.description: Final PRH decisions in national patent and utility-model matters may be appealed to the Market Court. The recipient of a decision may appeal if the decision is adverse to them. Appeals must be filed within 60 days of receiving the decision and a fixed fee must be paid when filing the appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A further appeal to the Supreme Administrative Court is possible against a Market Court decision only with leave granted by that court; the appeal to the Supreme Administrative Court must be filed within 30 days of the Market Court decision being notified (PatL 26, 27, 27a §; HmL 22, 23 §). Appeal instructions are attached to appealable decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post‑grant invalidation (nullity) and enforcement jurisdictions
rubrics_metrics.description: After PRH has granted a patent and the nine‑month opposition period has elapsed, the only way to revoke a patent nationally is to bring a nullity action in the Market Court. Patent owners must enforce their patents themselves; infringement suits are brought in Market Court or in the Unified Patent Court (UPC) for unitary/EP patents in applicable cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of time limits (post‑grant opposition window) and the competent fora: national actions in Market Court, UPC for unitary/EP patent matters. Patent owners should monitor and enforce infringements proactively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentable subject matter and exclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent may be granted for any invention in any field of technology that is industrially applicable, novel and inventive. Certain items are not regarded as inventions or are non‑patentable: discoveries, scientific theories, mathematical methods, artistic creations, schemes/rules/methods for intellectual activity, games or business methods, computer programs, presentation of information, surgical/therapeutic/diagnostic methods on humans/animals, plant varieties and animal breeds, essentially biological methods for breeding, discoveries of the human body or its constituent elements (including gene sequences) and inventions whose commercial exploitation is contrary to public order or morality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See PatL 1 § and related provisions; exclusions are interpreted with reference to guidance in chapter E (e.g., E.6, E.8).

rubrics_metrics.name: Application language, decision language and translation obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: A national patent application may be filed in Finnish, Swedish or English. PRH issues decisions in Finnish, Swedish or English. The choice of application language and decision language determines which translations must be supplied to PRH during processing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If filed in Finnish or Swedish, the decision language is the corresponding language and pending claims/abstract must be translated into the other national language before publication. If filed in English and applicant requests decisions in English, translations of the claims and abstract into Finnish or Swedish must be supplied before publication; the claims translation is a condition for provisional protection (PatL 60 § 1 mom.). If the applicant does not want English proceedings, a full translation into Finnish or Swedish must be provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic document (perusasiakirja) and limits on amendments
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'basic document' is the specification (with drawings) and the claims as they were included in the application on the filing date (in Finnish, Swedish or English as applicable). A patent application must not be amended so as to seek protection for subject‑matter that was not evident from the basic document as filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For PCT national phase continuations and nationalised EPs there are special rules defining which documents count as the basic document (PatL 13 §; PatA 21 §; PatL 31 § and PatM references). Any amendment adding matter beyond the basic document is disallowed; changes are treated per chapter H.3.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mandatory contents of the application form (hakemuskirja)
rubrics_metrics.description: The application form must be signed by the applicant or agent and must include: applicant's name, domicile and address; if represented, the representative's domicile and address; inventor's name and address; a short, matter‑of‑fact title of the invention; information on who is authorized to receive office communications if multiple applicants or representative is used; indication of any biological deposit under PatL 8a §; list of attachments; and a request if applicant wants decisions in English.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the application claims priority to an earlier application, the earlier application's date, country and number must be stated. If a biological deposit is involved, it must be stated on the form (PatA 2 §; PatA 10 §).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency of disclosure / enablement in the specification
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must describe the invention clearly and completely so that a person skilled in the art can understand the principle and carry out the invention without undue experimentation. The description must contain at least one sufficient example or embodiment enabling the invention across the claimed scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repetition of the invention must not rely on luck; the skilled person must be able to reach the same result by following the disclosure. Unnecessary details that belong to common general knowledge should not be included. For broad claim scope, the description must include enough exemplifying embodiments to reasonably cover the claimed scope (PatA 17 §; PatM 4 §). For general structural formulae defining compound groups, the specification must include sufficiently diverse examples to enable preparation of members not explicitly exemplified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification structure and required content
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must begin with a short, matter‑of‑fact title and comprise a general part and a particular part. The general part must state the field of the invention, the prior art known to the applicant (including patent publications and literature per WIPO ST.14) and what the invention achieves over the prior art, linking to the claims. The particular part explains the invention in detail, preferably using embodiments and referring to drawings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use fictitious names; trademarks are allowed only in exceptional cases and must be identified as trademarks (use ® for Finnish registered marks). If drawings are included, provide a list of all figures as an introduction to the particular part; text and drawings must be separate. Tables, chemical and mathematical formulae may be included in the text. Special requirements for biological materials and sequence listings are set out in chapter B.9.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trademarks and product identification in the specification
rubrics_metrics.description: Fictitious names must not be used. Registered trademarks may be used only in exceptional cases where no suitable established name exists; the specification must indicate that a trademark is used and a Finnish registered trademark must be marked (e.g., ®). The type of goods must always be stated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid relying on trademarks to define technical features because mark meanings may change over time (PatM 6 §).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequence listing and biological material special requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: If the invention includes nucleotide sequences of at least ten consecutive defined nucleotides or amino acid sequences of at least four consecutive defined amino acids, the specification must include a listing of such sequences. Special requirements for biological-material deposit and related descriptions are treated in B.9.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe the separate chapter B.9 for biological material deposit, sequence disclosures and related formalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims must be clear, precise, concise and intelligible
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventions must be presented in the claims in a manner that is understandable, clear, precise and concise. This requirement applies to individual claims (independent and dependent) and to the claim set as a whole. Claims determine the scope of protection; therefore concepts used should be, where possible, understandable by a skilled person from the claim language alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ambiguity in claim category or wording undermines the claimed scope. The claim wording should, if possible, define the category (product, device, method, use) and the technical features unambiguously (PatL 8 §).

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent claims must include all essential features
rubrics_metrics.description: Independent claims must present all essential features of the invention. A feature is essential if, from the specification, it is evident that the solution would not work in the asserted way without that feature. Implicit features known to be part of the general concept need not be recited explicitly (e.g., a car claim implicitly includes wheels).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not include merely wishful or optional features; essentiality is assessed by reference to the specification and how the invention functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional/effect‑defined claim limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims defined solely by the intended effect or result (functional/effect‑based) are generally not allowed. A claim using such definitions must make it clear how the intended effect is achieved and the means must be verifiable by a skilled person without inventive effort across the full claimed scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In rare special circumstances an effect‑based definition can be allowed if the specification and common general knowledge enable the skilled person to achieve the effect without inventive activity or undue experimentation across the scope (PatM guidance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative limitations (disclaimers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Negative claim limitations (disclaimers) which exclude parts of the otherwise defined scope are permitted in certain circumstances, primarily when the invention cannot be defined clearly and concisely by positive features or positive features would unreasonably limit the claim scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A disclaimer may be present in the original claim or added later (see amendment rules, H.3.2.5). Use disclaimers only when necessary to achieve clarity or appropriate scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim categories and how to formulate them
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed invention should, where possible, fall into product, apparatus/device, method or use categories. Products/devices are normally defined by composition or structural details; methods by steps or operations and, if necessary, devices and products used; uses by the specific purpose for which a product or method is used (PatM 14–17 §§).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the claim category that best reflects the technical contribution. Where product properties cannot otherwise be stated, product‑by‑process claim formats are acceptable for chemical products (product-by-process) but should be used properly with appropriate supporting disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product‑by‑process claims and chemical product guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: For products (especially chemical products) which are hard to define other than by their process of manufacture, product‑by‑process formulation is acceptable and may be accompanied by parameters to further define the product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using product‑by‑process claims, ensure the specification supports the product as distinct and provides sufficient disclosure of its preparation and properties (PatM 14 §).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of trademarks and standards in claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Trademarks are generally not used in claims because trademark meaning may change during the patent life. Internationally known trademarks may be used if their meaning is precise (examples: 'caterpillar belt', 'teflon', 'bluetooth'). If a standard is referred to, it must be sufficiently identified (publication date/version) and its use must not be merely wishful; the standard reference should define features precisely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a standard reference is to be part of a claim, identify the standard precisely. If the standard citation is wishful rather than defining, it will not normally be accepted as a limiting feature for inventive step (PatM guidance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative and approximate terms and parameters in claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Relative terms ('thin', 'strong', 'wide') are imprecise and not acceptable unless they constitute a known definition in the field. Approximate terms ('about', 'essentially', 'approximately') may be accepted depending on context; precision depends on whether their use prevents clear distinction from prior art. Parameters used in claims must be commonly used or their definition must be given in the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid vague relative terms unless the technical field provides a standard meaning; if approximate terms are used, ensure the context provides adequate precision so the claim remains distinguishable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of invention requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: An application must not seek a patent for two or more inventions that are not linked as a single general inventive concept. Inventions are considered linked if there is a technical relationship involving one or more common technical features which represent a contribution over the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unity assessment uses the presence of a common technical feature giving a technical contribution; see PatL 10 § and PatA 16 §. Effects of lack of unity on novelty search and national-phase PCT continuation are addressed in later chapters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim drafting formalities and prohibition of non‑technical matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Each patent claim must contain only one invention; claims must not include irrelevant or non‑technical information (for example, mentions of commercial advantage). Claims should include, where applicable, reference signs corresponding to the drawings (preferably in parentheses) but must be intelligible without them. Generic references like 'as described' are not accepted except in limited circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims may exceptionally refer directly to drawings' diagrams; chemical and mathematical formulae are allowed in claims but not drawings; tables may be included in claims only if clearly necessary for the invention (PatA 14 §; PatM 22–23 §).

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple independent claims within the same group — conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple independent claims in the same group (e.g., multiple independent product claims) are permitted only if: (1) the inventions are based on the same inventive concept; (2) they are technically closely related; and (3) it is evidently difficult to define the inventions sufficiently precisely, for example because of alternative embodiments that share common features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These criteria (PatM 19 §) must all be met to legitimately include several independent claims in the same category without raising unity objections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two‑part (preamble + characterising portion) claim format
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim should, where appropriate, be drafted in two parts: (1) a preamble indicating the title and prior art and (2) a characterising portion that specifies the novel and inventive features, typically introduced by wording like 'characterised in that' or 'known characterised by'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two‑part format is recommended whenever a clear distinction between known features and distinguishing features exists; exceptions and alternative single‑part formulations are allowed where two‑part form is artificial or misleading (PatA 14 §; PatM 12 §). The claim is assessed as a whole regardless of the partition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medical use claim drafting and 'for use' requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: First medical use claims (new therapeutic use of known substance) may be given product protection by phrasing as 'Substance X for use as a medicament' or 'Substance X for use in therapy/diagnostics/surgery'. Second (and further) medical uses are allowed by appropriate 'for use' formulations such as 'Substance X for use in the treatment of disease Y'. Dependent claims must also contain 'for use'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims phrased merely as 'use of X as a medicament' or similar are treated as method-of-treatment claims and may not be allowable under PatL 1 § 3rd paragraph; use the 'for use' wording to obtain product-type protection for medical uses (PatL 2 § 4–5 mom.; PatM 15 §). Acceptable claim examples are provided in the guidance (English examples also shown).

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawings requirements and conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Drawings must show all details necessary to understand the specification. The same reference numerals and letters must be used consistently in the description and drawings. Drawings must not contain markings other than those mentioned in the description and must avoid explanatory text except short words (e.g., water, steam, section A‑B). Block diagrams, flow charts and circuit diagrams may include explanatory text that aids understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid excessive detail that makes figures unclear. Figures are numbered consecutively (or with number/letter combos). Do not put descriptive text into drawings beyond short necessary labels (PatM 29–30 §).

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract: length, content and purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: The abstract is a short summary of the invention as disclosed in the specification, claims and drawings, intended to provide quick technical information. It must be no longer than 150 words, be based on the basic document, include the title and describe the technical problem and the main principle of the solution in easily understandable form. Chemical applications should include the chemical formula that best characterises the invention. The abstract must not contain statements of advantage or value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The abstract should enable readers to decide whether to consult the application/publication in full. If drawings are present, the applicant selects (or PRH may choose) a figure to publish with the abstract; reference numbers for illustrated features included in the abstract should be in parentheses. The applicant prepares the abstract and must file a translation in the other language in time before publication (PatA 18 §; PatM 26–27 §).

rubrics_metrics.name: Power of attorney, representative and transfer documentation requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: If the applicant has no domicile in Finland, they must have an agent resident in the European Economic Area entitled to represent the applicant in patent matters. When using an agent, a written power of attorney must be supplied stating: the agent's name, the application(s) covered (number and/or title), place and date, and the applicant's signature and printed name. Transfer documents must identify the transferee, the application concerned, place and date, and the transferor's signature and printed name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A power of attorney may be a copy. A power of attorney is not needed if the agent's name is in the application form and the applicant signed the form personally. To claim priority, a written request must be filed within 16 months of the priority date (PatA 10 § and related guidance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Formatting and layout requirements for specification, claims and abstract
rubrics_metrics.description: For paper filings (and electronic filings intended for equivalent printing), the specification, claims and abstract must be prepared in black on white A4 paper (or equivalent electronic format) in a single column with 1.5 line spacing. Font size must ensure capitals are at least 0.28 cm high (e.g., Times New Roman 12). Margins: left 2.5–4 cm, top 2–4 cm, right and bottom 2–3 cm. Text must be even, crisp and legible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pages of the specification and claims must be numbered consecutively starting from the beginning of the specification using Arabic numerals; numbers should be centered at least 2 cm from the top. Every fifth line of the specification and claims should be numbered at least 2.5 cm from the left margin (PatM 31 § guidance). Electronic filings must be formatted so printed output meets these requirements.
